entries.name: startswith_short_recv_int_arg-accept#0
entries.script: [J1] `Coll[Short](1,2).startsWith(ys)` where `ys` is declared `Coll[Short]` and evaluates to `Coll[Int](1)`: **`true`** at cost 85. `BoxesRunTime.equalsNumNum` widens every integral box, so Short-vs-Int compares equal by VALUE — the receiver's declared item type does not enter into it. Pairs with the S2 row's Byte-vs-Long: the widening is general.

entries.name: startswith_short_recv_short_arg-accept#1
entries.script: [J2] **CONTROL:** the well-typed argument also answers `true`, at cost 70.

entries.name: startswith_bigint_recv_long_arg-accept#2
entries.script: [J3] The same shape with a `Coll[BigInt]` receiver and a `Coll[Long](1)` argument of the same numeric value: **`false`** at cost 80. `CBigInt` is not a `java.lang.Number`, so `equalsNumNum` never runs and the boxed comparison simply fails. **The boundary of J1** — widening is not 'numeric equality' in general, it is the integral-box rule.

entries.name: startswith_bigint_recv_bigint_arg-accept#3
entries.script: [J4] **CONTROL:** the well-typed BigInt argument answers `true` at cost 65, so J3 is about the argument's runtime type and not about BigInt collections.

entries.name: startswith_nested_int_recv_long_arg-accept#4
entries.script: [J5] A NESTED receiver: `Coll[Coll[Int]](Coll(1)).startsWith(ys)` where `ys` evaluates to `Coll[Coll[Long]](Coll(1))` — equal inner values, different inner item type: **`false`** at cost 120. The elements are collections, so the comparison is `CollOverArray.equals`, which compares `tItem` BEFORE any item. The item-type gate from the collection-equality round, reached through startsWith.

entries.name: startswith_nested_int_recv_int_arg-accept#5
entries.script: [J6] **CONTROL:** the well-typed nested argument answers `true` at cost 105.

entries.name: endswith_nested_int_recv_long_arg-accept#6
entries.script: [J7] `endsWith` on the same pair answers `false` at the same cost 120 — with a single-item receiver the two ends coincide, so this pins that the verdict comes from the comparison and not from the end chosen.

entries.name: startswith_option_long_recv_option_int_arg-accept#7
entries.script: [J8] `Coll[Option[Long]](Global.some[Long](1))` — a generic collection over `[Lscala.Option;` — `.startsWith(ys)` where `ys` is declared `Coll[Option[Long]]` and evaluates to `Coll[Option[Int]](Global.some[Int](1))`: **`true`** at cost 108. The elements are `Option`s, so the boxed comparison is `Some.equals`, which compares its CONTENTS through `BoxesRunTime.equals` — and `1L == 1` there exactly as at the top level. The widening is not special to collection items; it follows Scala's `==` wherever the comparison lands.

entries.name: startswith_option_none_recv_none_int_arg-accept#8
entries.script: [J9] `None` against `None`, a `Coll[Option[Long]]` receiver and a `Coll[Option[Int]]` argument: **`true`** at cost 98. `None` is a singleton, so the declared type parameter cannot enter into it — the one row where the two item types are indistinguishable by construction.

entries.name: startswith_option_some_recv_none_int_arg-accept#9
entries.script: [J10] `Some(1L)` against the Int-typed `None`: **`false`** at cost 103 — so J8/J9 are value equality and not a blanket acceptance of `Option` items.

entries.name: startswith_option_none_recv_some_int_arg-accept#10
entries.script: [J11] The mirror: `None` against `Some(1)`, **`false`** at cost 103. With J10 it pins the answer to the ELEMENTS rather than to which side carries the lie.

entries.name: startswith_option_some_long_control-accept#11
entries.script: [J12] **CONTROL:** the honest `Coll[Option[Long]](Some(1L))` argument answers `true` at cost 93. J8's 108 is the `If` that carries the lie, not the comparison.

entries.name: startswith_option_none_long_control-accept#12
entries.script: [J13] **CONTROL:** an honest `None` argument against the `Some(1L)` receiver answers `false` at cost 88.

entries.name: startswith_option_some_long_2_control-accept#13
entries.script: [J14] **CONTROL:** `Some(2L)` answers `false` at cost 93 — same types, different value, so J12's `true` is the value's doing and not the shape's.

entries.name: eq_option_long_option_int-accept#14
entries.script: [J15] **THE ASYMMETRY, one level down:** `EQ` on the SAME two collections answers **`false`** at cost 94 where `startsWith` answers `true` (J8). `DataValueComparer` bails on the runtime item type before it reaches any item (`:323`, the collection-equality round), while `startsWith` reaches Scala's `==`. The split the census found for scalars, now with `Option` items: the SITE decides, not the values.
